name: Biology: phylogenetic topology recovery from simulated sequences
description: Reconstruct the unrooted tree topology of twenty simulated instances with 8 to 32 taxa and 250 to 2000 sites, generated inside the evaluator under the Jukes-Cantor model with hidden random topologies and branch lengths. The score is the mean normalized Robinson-Foulds distance to the generating trees.

sources.locator: Saitou and Nei (1987): the neighbour-joining method for reconstructing phylogenetic trees, the problem this task scores and the basis of the seed program.
Huelsenbeck (1995), Performance of phylogenetic methods in simulation: evaluating tree-reconstruction accuracy on sequences simulated along known trees, the protocol followed here.
Robinson and Foulds (1981): the split-based tree distance used as the score.
Guindon et al. (2010), PhyML 3.0: maximum-likelihood tree search, the state of practice a candidate would have to match or beat.

requirements.datasets: None downloaded; instances are generated deterministically inside the evaluator.

evaluation.benchmark: Biology: phylogenetic topology recovery from simulated sequences
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: reconstruct(sequences) -> Newick string over the labels t0..t(n-1) (branch lengths optional, trailing semicolon optional, every taxon exactly once). sequences maps those labels to equal-length DNA strings over ACGT simulated along an unknown tree. reconstruct is called once per instance in a sandboxed subprocess with a 180 s CPU budget for all 20 instances (8 to 32 taxa, 250 to 2000 sites). Score (minimize): mean normalized Robinson-Foulds distance between the non-trivial unrooted splits of the returned tree and those of the generating tree; 0 means recovering every topology exactly

limitations: Sequences are simulated under Jukes-Cantor with no rate heterogeneity, no indels and no model misspecification, so the task measures reconstruction under an idealized model rather than on real data.
Instances, topologies and branch-length regimes are a local choice (20 instances, 8 to 32 taxa); results do not transfer automatically to empirical alignments.
Exact recovery is not guaranteed to be attainable from finite data, so the minimum achievable score is unknown and the seed's value is only a baseline.
Branch lengths of the returned tree are ignored: only the unrooted topology is scored.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published value for this instance set. The neighbour-joining seed reaches mean normalized Robinson-Foulds 0.177 and recovers 5 of the 20 topologies exactly; maximum-likelihood search is expected to do better, which is the intended research content.

sources.title: Performance of phylogenetic methods in simulation

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Recover the evolutionary tree relating a set of sequences from the sequences alone.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Tree reconstruction underpins comparative biology, and its accuracy under known generating trees is the standard way methods such as neighbour joining and maximum likelihood have been compared since the 1990s.

papers.title: The neighbor-joining method: a new method for reconstructing phylogenetic trees
papers.primary_goal: Develop a method that reconstructs the correct phylogenetic tree from sequence data.
papers.task_relation: The task scores exactly this reconstruction problem; the seed program is a neighbour-joining implementation.

papers.title: Performance of phylogenetic methods in simulation
papers.primary_goal: Measure how often phylogenetic methods recover the true tree from sequences simulated along known trees.
papers.task_relation: The task follows this protocol: simulated sequences, hidden true topology, distance to it as the score.

science_relevance.reason: Both papers' main research goal is phylogenetic tree reconstruction and its accuracy, which the evaluator measures with the Robinson-Foulds distance to the generating tree.
science_relevance.verification_basis: Crossref metadata inspected; simulator determinism, split counts, Newick parsing and the distance metric checked by unit tests.
